title: Breast abscess and lactational mastitis
subtitle: Keep feeding, aspirate before you cut

sources.title: ABM Clinical Protocol #36: The Mastitis Spectrum, Revised 2022 (Mitchell KB, Johnson HM, Rodriguez JM et al., Breastfeed Med)
Treatment of breast infection (Dixon JM, Khan LR)

red_flags.text: Systemic sepsis: hypotension, tachycardia, rigors or confusion.
Skin necrosis or a rapidly spreading erythema: necrotising infection is rare but must be recognised.
Inflammation in a woman who is not breastfeeding, especially if older, or that fails to settle on appropriate antibiotics: inflammatory breast cancer must be excluded by biopsy.
Recurrent periareolar abscess in a smoker: periductal mastitis and a mammary duct fistula.
A fluctuant mass that persists after a course of antibiotics.

do_now.text: Continue breastfeeding from both breasts on demand. Do not advise stopping; abrupt cessation increases the risk of abscess.
Avoid deep breast massage and excessive pumping to 'empty' the breast; use ice, supportive measures and an anti-inflammatory analgesic such as ibuprofen.

Start antibiotics if symptoms do not improve within 12 to 24 hours of these measures, or sooner if the woman is acutely unwell. Choose an anti-staphylococcal agent compatible with breastfeeding, per local protocol.
Septic patient: cultures, IV antibiotics per local sepsis protocol, and urgent surgical review.

assess.text: Breastfeeding history: latch, frequency, pumping, nipple damage, and any recent change in feeding pattern.
Examine for a fluctuant or tender mass, skin changes and axillary nodes. Fluctuance is often absent in a deep abscess.
Non-lactational infection: smoking, diabetes, periareolar location and previous episodes.

investigate.text: Breast ultrasound for any suspected abscess or failure to improve within 48 hours of antibiotics.
Culture of milk or pus, especially in hospital-acquired, recurrent or non-resolving infection, and where MRSA is prevalent.
Core biopsy for any persistent mass or inflammation outside lactation.

resuscitate.text: Adjust antibiotics to culture; consider MRSA cover where local prevalence or culture suggests it.
Treat sepsis with fluids and IV antibiotics while arranging drainage.

definitive.text: Breast abscess: ultrasound-guided needle aspiration, repeated as required, with antibiotics. This is first-line and usually avoids an incision.
Incision and drainage when the overlying skin is thin or necrotic, the abscess is large or multiloculated, or repeated aspiration fails. Place the incision to allow continued breastfeeding.
Breastfeeding can continue from the affected side after drainage unless the incision is close to the nipple; express that side if it is.
Recurrent periductal abscess or mammary duct fistula: definitive excision of the affected duct system electively, once the acute infection has settled; advise smoking cessation.

escalate.text: Breast surgical team for any abscess, any non-lactational infection and any inflammation that does not settle.
Lactation support or midwifery for every lactating woman: feeding technique is part of the treatment.
Breast clinic for imaging and biopsy of any residual mass after the infection has resolved.

notes: Mastitis is now understood as a spectrum driven by ductal inflammation and oedema. Advice to massage hard and empty the breast often makes it worse.
Aspiration before incision: most lactational abscesses resolve with repeated needle aspiration, leaving no scar and no interruption to feeding.
A red breast that has not settled after two courses of antibiotics is a cancer until a biopsy says otherwise.
